analysis.one_liner: Shortens how long bad marks stay on credit reports and scrubs debts from fraud, predatory lending, medical bills, and abuse.
analysis.headline: Introduced by one representative with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on June 24, 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Fair Credit Reporting Act to clean up credit reports. It would cut the years that bankruptcies, judgments, and other negative items stay on a report, force credit bureaus to remove paid or settled debts within 45 days, keep most medical debt off reports entirely, and wipe out the credit damage from fraudulent or predatory loans -- including private student loans at for-profit colleges -- and from financial abuse by a spouse or family member. It would also require the three big credit bureaus to give free credit monitoring and identity theft protection to fraud victims, unemployed people, public assistance recipients, active-duty military, and people 65 and older. The bill died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose credit reports carry negative marks: victims of identity theft and fraud, survivors of domestic financial abuse, people with medical debt, borrowers defrauded by for-profit colleges, and people who went through foreclosure or predatory mortgage servicing. Nearly one in five consumers has a medical collection on their report, and the bill's findings cite research showing paid medical debt can knock 10 to 22 points off a score even after it is paid.

how_it_helps.text: Shortens the clock on negative credit information: bankruptcies fall off after 7 years instead of 10, and most other adverse items, suits, and judgments after 4 years instead of 7 [S3].
Requires credit bureaus to remove fully paid or settled debts from a report within 45 days of payment [S3].

Bars most medical debt from appearing on reports at all for the first year, prohibits reporting debt from medically necessary procedures, and requires rapid removal of paid or settled medical collections [S3].

Wipes adverse credit information from the reports of borrowers whose loans involved a lender's fraudulent, discriminatory, or deceptive practices -- including private student loans at for-profit colleges with documented fraud -- once the Consumer Bureau or a court certifies the claim [S3].

Lets victims of financial abuse by a spouse, family member, caregiver, or dating partner get a court order to remove the abuser's fraudulent debt from their credit report, without needing a police report [S3].

Gives free credit monitoring and identity theft protection to fraud victims, unemployed job seekers, public assistance recipients, active-duty military and National Guard members, and people 65 or older, and strengthens fraud alerts and credit freezes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The three nationwide credit bureaus (Equifax, TransUnion, Experian) would lose reporting fees and face tighter accuracy duties; debt collectors and debt buyers would lose the leverage of reporting accounts; private student loan holders and predatory mortgage servicers would lose the ability to report on loans tainted by fraud; for-profit colleges would face students whose defrauded debts vanish from credit records; and paid credit monitoring services would face a free public alternative.

drawbacks.text: Lenders and landlords would see less information: shorter reporting periods and mandatory removal of paid debts mean less payment history to judge applicants, which the bill's own findings acknowledge is the system's underwriting value -- some borrowers could face higher prices or tighter credit as lenders price for the added uncertainty [S3].

The bill hands the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau broad rulemaking over credit scoring and reporting, and voids any contract provision that circumvents its purposes, which industry would call an overreach that raises compliance costs [S3].

Blanket limits on medical debt reporting ignore cases where unpaid medical bills are a genuine signal of financial distress, though the findings cite CFPB research that medical collections predict default far less than other collections [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers with medical debt, fraud-stained reports, or defrauded student loans, the benefits are substantial and targeted at documented harms the credit bureaus had failed to fix on their own. The main cost falls on lenders, who would have less information to underwrite credit; that could raise prices at the margin, but it is the kind of tradeoff every consumer protection law makes. On balance the bill helps the people it names and costs concentrated industry interests.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee from June 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023 without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Representative Rashida Tlaib introduced the bill on June 24, 2021 [S1].
No member of the House cosponsored it [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the 117th Congress [S5].
The 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023, and the bill expired without coming to a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus, debt collectors, private student loan holders, and for-profit colleges kept the existing credit reporting rules, which the bill's findings described as systematically loading inaccurate and unfair information onto consumers' reports. Consumers with damaged credit got no relief.

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Financial Services Committee; no other member cosponsored it

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair Maxine Waters)
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair, House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral -- no hearing, markup, or floor consideration was scheduled before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: With zero cosponsors, no committee action, and no roll-call votes, the record shows nothing about how the parties would have lined up.

industries.note: The bill would force faster deletion of adverse information, ban reporting most medical debt and medically necessary procedure debt, and require free credit monitoring for millions of consumers, cutting into the reporting and monitoring revenue these firms earn from selling data about people who cannot opt out of being tracked.

Paid or settled debts would have to come off reports within 45 days and medical collections would face a one-year waiting period, removing the collection tradeline leverage collectors rely on to push people to pay. The findings note collectors currently decide on their own when and how long to report a debt.

industries.industry: Private student loan holders and predatory mortgage lenders/servicers
industries.note: Adverse information tied to loans involving a lender's fraud, discrimination, or deceptive practices would be wiped from borrowers' reports after certification, and lawsuits by private education loan holders would stop appearing on reports after credit restoration.

Borrowers defrauded by proprietary schools would be certified by the CFPB and have the loan's adverse credit information removed, reducing the collections pressure that keeps defaulted for-profit students paying on worthless credentials.

The bill would mandate free credit monitoring and identity theft protection for fraud victims, the unemployed, public assistance recipients, military members, and seniors -- a free public alternative to the $120-$300 a year services the findings say about 50 million Americans were already buying.
